questions.q: What is the key difference between "caste influencing politics" and "politics influencing caste"? Give one example of each.
questions.a: "Caste influencing politics" means pre-existing caste groups pressure parties for tickets/policies (e.g., Jats demanding OBC status). "Politics influencing caste" means parties/create new caste categories or mobilise latent identities for votes (e.g., BSP creating "Bahujan" identity). A wrong answer that gives the same example for both reveals the student sees the relationship as one-way only.

questions.q: Why did the Mandal Commission recommendation (1990) transform "Other Backward Classes" from a bureaucratic list into a cohesive political force?
questions.a: The 27% reservation in central jobs gave diverse castes a shared material interest in maintaining the OBC label, prompting leaders to organise across traditional boundaries. A wrong answer focusing only on "caste solidarity" misses the crucial role of state policy in creating the incentive for political mobilisation.

questions.q: A regional party in Bihar announces a new "Most Backward Classes" quota within the existing OBC quota just before state elections. Analyse this move using the concept of "politics influencing caste".
questions.a: The party is fragmenting the OBC category to isolate a smaller, more loyal vote bank — a classic case of politics reshaping caste boundaries for electoral gain. A wrong answer that calls this "social justice" without mentioning electoral calculation shows inability to see political strategy behind policy design.

questions.q: Compare how the Congress party's "rainbow coalition" (1950s-80s) and the BSP's "Bahujan" strategy (1990s onwards) differently used caste identities for political mobilisation.
questions.a: Congress accommodated dominant castes (Brahmins, Dalits, Muslims) without challenging hierarchy; BSP actively constructed a new pan-caste "Bahujan" identity opposing upper castes. A wrong answer that says "both used caste" misses the qualitative difference: one managed existing identities, the other engineered a new oppositional identity.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Caste-based political mobilisation has strengthened Indian democracy by giving voice to marginalised groups." Provide two arguments for and two against.
questions.a: For: Enabled representation (Article 330/332), forced parties to address lower-caste demands. Against: Entrenched caste as primary political identity, encouraged vote-bank politics over issue-based debate, sometimes led to intra-caste violence. A wrong answer that only lists positives shows uncritical acceptance; one that only lists negatives ignores historical exclusion.

questions.q: Design a hypothetical election manifesto promise for a new party that wants to mobilise "Pasmanda Muslims" (backward Muslim castes) without reinforcing religious communalism. Explain how your promise navigates the caste-religion intersection.
questions.a: A strong answer proposes sub-quota within OBC for Pasmandas (like Bihar's 2005 model), cites Sachar Committee data, and frames it as intra-Muslim social justice — not Muslim vs Hindu. A poor answer either ignores caste within Muslims or proposes religion-based quota (unconstitutional under Article 15(1)), revealing confusion between caste and religious categories.
